units.title: Sequential decisions, contextual bandits and the agent-environment boundary
outcomes: Explain how supervised prediction, contextual bandits and full RL differ in whether actions change future situations.
Draw the agent-environment loop and name what belongs to the agent and what belongs to the environment.
Decide whether a new task is a bandit, a contextual bandit or a sequential MDP and state what information the policy may use.
units.why: Supervised learning predicts a label for a fixed input. RL chooses actions that change what happens next. If the boundary is drawn in the wrong place, later values optimize the wrong loop.

next.note: Carry the boundary into state and Markov definitions.
Keep reward and boundary questions for the formulation unit.

study.title: Two slot machines and three policies
study.locator: Two Slot Machines and Three Policies, Three Outcomes with the 60 percent and 40 percent machines and expected rewards 0.2 and minus 0.2 (page read 2026-10-14)

focus: Supervised learning uses fixed input-output pairs. RL uses trial and error with delayed consequences. Bandits remove state change to isolate exploration.
The agent selects \(A_t\) from \(S_t\). The environment returns \(R_{t+1}\) and \(S_{t+1}\). Everything outside the agent is the environment.
Contextual bandits add a context that selects the payoff table, but actions still affect only immediate reward. Full RL lets actions change the next situation.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, draw the loop with \(S_t\), \(A_t\), \(R_{t+1}\) and \(S_{t+1}\) and compute expected per-pull rewards for 60 percent and 40 percent machines with plus 1 and minus 1 rewards, then totals for uniform random and always-A over 100 rounds: 0.2 and minus 0.2 per pull, 0 and 20 in total.
traps: Treating a contextual bandit as full RL and adding discounting and bootstrapping where no next state exists.
Drawing the boundary so the agent owns the reward function or the physics. The environment owns dynamics and reward. The agent owns the policy and value estimates.
Assuming greedy action selection solves exploration. With 10 pulls each on 60 versus 40, about 0.128 of experiments rank the worse arm first, so exploitation inherits estimation error.

selfTest.q: When is a task a contextual bandit rather than full RL?
selfTest.a: When a context selects the payoff table but the action affects only immediate reward and not the next situation. Full RL lets actions change the next state.

selfTest.q: Who owns what in Sutton Figure 3.1?
selfTest.a: The agent owns the policy and value estimates. The environment owns the dynamics \(p\) and the reward. State and reward pass from environment to agent. Action passes back.

selfTest.q: What are the expected totals for uniform random and always-A over 100 rounds on the 60 versus 40 machines?
selfTest.a: Uniform random gives 0 per round and 0 in total. Always-A gives 0.2 per round and 20 in total.

selfTest.q: Why can 10 pulls each still pick the worse machine?
selfTest.a: Small-sample noise can reverse the order. About 0.128 of experiments give more wins to B than to A, so committing to the observed winner locks in the mistake.

units.title: States, observations, the Markov property, transition kernels and rewards
outcomes: Explain the Markov property with \(p(S_{t+1} \mid S_t, A_t) = p(S_{t+1} \mid H_t, A_t)\) and give a non-Markov observation example.
Write the dynamics \(p(s', r \mid s, a)\) and derive \(p(s' \mid s, a)\), \(r(s, a)\) and \(r(s, a, s')\) by marginalization.
Distinguish state, observation and history and state what must be added to restore Markov structure.
units.why: Values condition on state. If the state omits history the learner needs, Bellman updates average over different situations as if they were one.

next.note: Carry transitions and rewards into returns and horizons.
Use states to define values and advantages.

study.title: MDP tuple with bandit, CartPole and LLM table
study.locator: The MDP Tuple: State, Action, Transition Dynamics and Reward Function with the bandit, CartPole and LLM table and the CartPole 4D state example (page read 2026-10-14)

focus: Markov means the future is independent of the past given the present. History \(H_t\) collapses to \(S_t\).
The four-argument \(p(s', r \mid s, a)\) sums to 1 over \(s'\) and \(r\) for each \(s\) and \(a\). Other quantities come from summing out \(r\) or \(s'\).
Observation is what the agent receives. State is what determines what happens next. If \(S_t = O_t\) is insufficient, augment with history, velocity, time remaining or belief.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write \(p(s' \mid s, a)\) and \(r(s, a)\) from \(p(s', r \mid s, a)\) and show the normalization sums to 1. Use a toy where one action gives \((s'_1, r=1)\) with 0.7 and \((s'_2, r=0)\) with 0.3, so \(p(s'_1 \mid s, a) = 0.7\) and \(r(s, a) = 0.7\).
traps: Calling an observation a Markov state because it looks complete. CartPole angle without angular velocity is the standard counterexample on the Hands-on page.
Normalizing \(p\) over the wrong axis. Sum over \(s'\) and \(r\), not over \(s\) and \(a\).
Treating deterministic physics as a known model. Unknown \(P\) is the usual case. Planning assumes known \(P\) only as a baseline.

selfTest.q: State the Markov property in one equation.
selfTest.a: The state \(S_t\) is Markov when \(p(S_{t+1} \mid S_t, A_t) = p(S_{t+1} \mid H_t, A_t)\). The future depends on history only through the present state and action.

selfTest.q: How do you get \(r(s, a)\) from \(p(s', r \mid s, a)\)?
selfTest.a: Weight each reward by its probability and sum out the next state: \(r(s, a) = \sum_{s', r} r p(s', r \mid s, a)\).

selfTest.q: Why is angle-only CartPole not Markov?
selfTest.a: The same angle with different angular velocities leads to different next angles. Add velocity to restore the property.

selfTest.q: How is a bandit an MDP?
selfTest.a: It has a single state. The transition always returns to that state. Actions affect only immediate reward.

study.title: Assignment 1 horizon questions
study.locator: Section 1, Effect of Effective Horizon, parts (a) to (d), pp. 1 to 2; inventory MDP with horizon \(H\) versus discount \(\gamma\)
study.depth: Answer on paper. Do not start the RiverSwim code here.

focus: Episodic tasks end in terminal states. Continuing tasks have no terminal. Finite-horizon tasks stop after \(H\) steps even without a terminal.
Termination means \(V = 0\) after. Truncation means keep \(\gamma V(S')\). Code must use \((1 - terminated)\), not \((1 - done)\).

In Gymnasium 1.4.0 a single `Env` needs manual `reset` after done. `SyncVectorEnv` with default `NEXT_STEP` returns the true final first, then a fake autoreset step with reward 0 and both flags false. Never store that step as a transition.
units.reproduce: With `gymnasium.make("CartPole-v1", max_episode_steps=5)` and `env.reset(seed=0)`, show step 5 ends with `terminated=False` and `truncated=True`. With a 2-env `SyncVectorEnv` show step 5 has reward 1 with truncation true, then step 6 has reward 0 with both flags false.
traps: Using `done = terminated or truncated` to cut the bootstrap. Truncation must still bootstrap.
Storing the `NEXT_STEP` autoreset transition. Its observation is the reset state and its reward is 0. It is not a transition.
Adding remaining time to the observation for external truncation. The tutorial reserves that fix for finite-horizon inherent limits.

selfTest.q: With \(\gamma = 0.5\) and rewards 1, 2, 6, 3, 2 over 5 steps, what are \(G_0\) to \(G_5\)?
With \(\gamma = 0.9\) and reward 2 then infinite 7s, what are \(G_1\) and \(G_0\)?
What is the correct one-step value target at termination versus truncation?
selfTest.a: At termination use \(r\). At truncation use \(r + \gamma V(S')\). In code use `vf_target = rew + gamma * (1 - terminated) * vf_next_state`.

selfTest.q: What does the vector step after done return under the default mode?
selfTest.a: Reward 0 with both flags false and the reset observation. Skip it in buffers and losses.
